title: Solve a Crime with Fake Blood Spatter!
summary:
Have you ever watched a detective show and seen them study blood splatters at a crime scene? It's not just TV magic—it's real science called forensic science. Forensic scientists look at blood drops to figure out what happened. They measure the size of the spatter to learn how far the blood fell. Now you can try it yourself with fake blood!

In this experiment, you'll make your own fake blood using corn syrup and red food coloring. Then you'll drop it from different heights—like 10 centimeters, 50 centimeters, or even 100 centimeters—and measure the splatter. Does a drop from higher up make a bigger splat? You might think so, but you'll have to test it to be sure. The word 'forensic' comes from ancient Rome, where people argued cases in a public forum. Today, forensic scientists use math and science to help solve crimes. They stay fair and look at all the evidence to find the truth.

This project is for kids who like mysteries and science. It's quick—you can do it in a day—and the materials are easy to find. Just remember, this topic can be a little scary because it's about blood, even if it's fake. If you're squeamish, you might want to pick a different experiment. But if you're ready to be a junior detective, grab some corn syrup and start investigating! Who knows? You might discover how blood spatter can tell a story.
why_it_matters: This shows you that science isn't just in a lab—it can help solve real mysteries, and even a simple experiment at home can teach you how to think like a detective.

background_read: In real life, forensic scientists are often called to crime scenes to collect tiny bits of evidence like hair, fibers, or blood drops.
They use math to measure the angle and size of blood spatters; a long, narrow stain might mean the blood hit the surface at a low angle, like when someone was moving.
Blood spatter analysis helped solve famous cases, such as figuring out whether a death was an accident or on purpose.

The topic of blood, even if fake, might feel too scary or gross for some children, so they might prefer other science projects.
This is a perfect taste of what crime scene investigators do, blending math and curiosity to uncover hidden stories in tiny details.
